hood_landmark.Mission District: Mission Dolores, the city's oldest building, plus Balmy Alley murals
hood_landmark.Haight-Ashbury: the iconic Haight and Ashbury intersection of 1960s counterculture fame
hood_landmark.Chinatown: the Dragon Gate at Grant Avenue and Bush Street
hood_landmark.The Castro: the Castro Theatre's landmark neon marquee

avoid.reason: The Tenderloin and parts of SoMa/Mid-Market have open drug use and aggressive panhandling day and night.

hood_desc: The Mission is a lively, sunny, historically Latino neighborhood packed with taquerias, murals, dive bars and trendy restaurants, great for foodies, young creatives and nightlife seekers.

Haight-Ashbury is the storied birthplace of 1960s hippie counterculture, now a bohemian strip of vintage clothing shops, record stores and Victorians beside Golden Gate Park, appealing to music lovers and free spirits.
Nob Hill is an elegant, hilly enclave of grand historic hotels, cathedrals and cable cars with sweeping views, suiting upscale travelers who want refined, quiet surroundings near downtown.
Chinatown is one of the oldest and busiest Chinatowns in North America, a dense warren of dim sum halls, herb shops and temples that draws visitors wanting authentic food and cultural immersion.

The Castro is the world-famous heart of LGBTQ life in San Francisco, a vibrant, welcoming district of rainbow flags, bars, cafes and the historic Castro Theatre, ideal for the queer community and open-minded visitors.

water.note: Tap water is safe and known for its high quality Hetch Hetchy source.

transit.pay: The Clipper card works on BART, Muni, ferries and more - get it free in Apple/Google Wallet or as a plastic card ($3) from station machines and Walgreens. Contactless tap-to-pay with your own bank card is also rolling out across Muni and BART. Cable cars cost $8 a ride (Clipper, app, or cash to the conductor).
transit.hours: BART runs about 5am-midnight (from 6am Sat, 8am Sun); Muni runs roughly 5am-midnight with 24-hour Owl bus routes; cable cars about 7am-10:30pm.

transit.m: BART train direct to downtown (~30 min)

food.name: Sourdough bread
food.desc: Tangy, blistered loaves leavened by wild yeasts that thrive in the city's cool fog. Some starters here date back to the Gold Rush.

places.name: Tartine Bakery
places.note: The modern gold standard; mahogany-crusted country loaf, released at set times and often sold out.

places.name: Boudin Bakery
places.note: The city's oldest continuously operating business, using a mother dough alive since 1849; watch the bakers work.

places.name: Acme Bread Company
places.note: Handy Ferry Building counter for a superb loaf to eat on the waterfront.

food.name: Cioppino
food.desc: Tomato-and-wine seafood stew invented by Italian fishermen on the wharf, packed with Dungeness crab, clams, mussels and prawns.

places.name: Sotto Mare
places.note: Famously enormous bowl billed for two, arriving as a crimson tide of shellfish; expect to queue.

places.name: Tadich Grill
places.note: California's oldest restaurant, open since 1849; cioppino is the top seller, about 27,000 bowls a year.

places.name: Anchor Oyster Bar
places.note: Tiny marble counter, no reservations, and a beautifully clean version of the stew.

food.name: Mission burrito
food.desc: Foil-wrapped, steamed-tortilla behemoth with rice, beans, meat, salsa and crema. Invented in the Mission in the 1960s and copied worldwide.

places.name: El Farolito
places.note: Widely rated the best in the city; super burrito with carne asada, cash only, open past 1am.

places.name: La Taqueria
places.note: James Beard classic, famously no rice; ask for it dorado, griddled crisp on the outside.

places.name: Taqueria Cancun
places.note: The late-night workhorse; the burrito mojado with grilled onions is the local order.

food.name: Dim sum
food.desc: Har gow, siu mai and char siu bao in the oldest Chinatown in North America, from bakery takeout windows to white-tablecloth trolley service.

places.name: Good Mong Kok Bakery
places.note: Shoebox takeout counter with a daily queue; generously stuffed char siu bao for a couple of dollars. Cash preferred.

places.name: Yank Sing
places.note: Michelin Bib Gourmand; the airy Spear Street branch does excellent xiao long bao and scallop siu mai.

places.name: Hong Kong Lounge II
places.note: Where locals go instead of Chinatown; sharper cooking and a huge weekend crowd, so book.

food.name: Dungeness crab
food.desc: Sweet local crab, cracked cold with lemon or served as a Louie salad. Season generally runs from mid-November through spring.

places.name: Swan Oyster Depot
places.note: Open since 1912; 18 counter stools, no reservations. Crab Louie and the crab back are the legendary orders.

places.name: Scoma's
places.note: Pier-side classic with its own fish receiving station; the tourist wharf pick that locals still respect.

food.name: Irish coffee
food.desc: Hot coffee, Irish whiskey, sugar and a float of lightly whipped cream. It was introduced to America in San Francisco in 1952.

places.name: The Buena Vista Cafe
places.note: The birthplace, serving around 2,000 a day in an unbroken assembly line at the bar. Recipe unchanged since 1952.

places.name: Comstock Saloon
places.note: Victorian-era saloon making a more refined version alongside excellent classic cocktails.

food.name: Craft beer
food.desc: Hop-forward West Coast IPAs and small-batch experiments. Anchor Brewing shut in 2023 and its taproom is gone, but independent taprooms still thrive.

places.name: Cellarmaker Brewing Co
places.note: Arguably the city's most loved brewery; constantly rotating small-batch hoppy beers, plus a pizza taproom.

places.name: Fort Point Beer Company
places.note: Locally ubiquitous; the hazy IPA and KSA are the ones to try, with a handy Ferry Building outpost.

places.name: 21st Amendment Brewery
places.note: Big, lively brewpub near Oracle Park; ideal before or after a Giants game.

landmarks: Golden Gate Bridge
The iconic International Orange suspension bridge spanning the Golden Gate strait, one of the most photographed bridges in the world.
Alcatraz Island
The former federal penitentiary on a rocky island in San Francisco Bay, famous for its history and stunning bay views.
Fisherman's Wharf
A bustling waterfront district known for sea lions, seafood, and views of the bay and Alcatraz.
Painted Ladies
A row of colorful Victorian houses along Alamo Square, framed by the downtown skyline, a favorite photo spot.
Lombard Street
The famously steep, winding one-block section of street with eight hairpin turns, known as the 'crookedest street in the world'.
San Francisco Cable Cars
The city's historic, hand-operated cable car system, a moving National Historic Landmark and quintessential SF photo subject.
Coit Tower
An Art Deco tower atop Telegraph Hill offering panoramic views of the city and bay, decorated with Depression-era murals.
Golden Gate Park
A vast urban park featuring the Japanese Tea Garden and Conservatory of Flowers, a green escape in the heart of the city.
Ferry Building
A historic 1898 waterfront landmark with its clock tower, now home to a popular marketplace and farmers market.
Twin Peaks
Twin hills offering one of the best panoramic viewpoints over the entire city, bay, and Golden Gate Bridge.

train.note: No international trains, and Amtrak's long-distance routes (California Zephyr, Coast Starlight, San Joaquins) actually leave from Emeryville and Oakland across the bay - free Amtrak Thruway buses connect from the Salesforce Transit Center downtown and are included in the ticket, but allow about 30 minutes for the transfer. Caltrain (https://www.caltrain.com/) runs electrified regional trains to Palo Alto and San Jose from 4th & King, and BART (https://www.bart.gov/) links downtown with Oakland, Berkeley and both airports. Sleepers on the Zephyr and Coast Starlight sell out months ahead in summer, so book early.

bus.note: No direct international coaches from San Francisco; Tijuana or Vancouver means changing in Los Angeles or Seattle. Greyhound (https://www.greyhound.com/), FlixBus (https://www.flixbus.com/) and Megabus (https://us.megabus.com/) serve cities across California and the western US from the Salesforce Transit Center at 425 Mission Street, with Los Angeles taking 8-9 hours and Sacramento about 2. FlixBus and Megabus sell tickets online only, and advance fares are a fraction of the walk-up price.

intl.to: Oakland, Alameda, Richmond & Vallejo (USA) - from the Ferry Building and Pier 41
Sausalito & Larkspur (USA) - from the Ferry Building
Angel Island & Sausalito (USA) - from Pier 41 at Fisherman's Wharf

ferry.note: No international ferries, but the bay network is genuinely useful transport. San Francisco Bay Ferry and Golden Gate Ferry run from the Ferry Building at the foot of Market Street and from Pier 41 - Sausalito takes about 30 minutes, Oakland 25 and Vallejo an hour. Fares are cheapest with a Clipper card and no advance booking is needed, though Angel Island sailings can be busy on summer weekends. Commuter routes such as Richmond and Harbor Bay run a much thinner timetable at weekends, so check before relying on them.

half.name: Napa Valley
half.blurb: California's famous wine country pairs hundreds of vineyards with rolling hills and celebrated tasting rooms.

half.name: Sonoma
half.blurb: A laid-back wine region with historic plazas, redwood groves and countless family-run vineyards to explore.

half.name: Muir Woods
half.blurb: Towering coastal redwoods shade quiet trails just north of the Golden Gate Bridge.

half.name: Sausalito
half.blurb: A charming waterfront town reached by ferry, with harbor views, galleries and seaside cafes.

half.name: Monterey
half.blurb: Coastal town known for its aquarium, historic Cannery Row and rugged Pacific shoreline.

half.name: Half Moon Bay
half.blurb: A relaxed coastal escape with wide beaches, bluff trails and a small-town harbor.
